questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presented with dysuria, urinary frequency, and fevers. He had a history of spinal injury and required intermittent self-catheterization. He had previously had recurrent urinary tract infections and ciprofloxacin-associated tendinopathy. On examination he was unwell. His temperature was 38.5°C and his heart rate 120 beats/min. Rectal examination revealed a very tender prostate.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric treatment?
questions.explanation: Meropenem This man has acute prostatitis and is systemically unwell. He has a history of recurrent catheterization-associated urinary tract infection and will not tolerate FLQ. In addition, he may be at risk of a drug-resistant Pseudomonas species, and so a carbapenem is a reasonable initial regimen. Ertapenem will not cover Pseudomonas. Treatment for STI is not appropriate as first line in this clinical context. Also considering the patient’s age and background history, a focus on Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas is more appropriate.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q22

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presented with a history of recurrent lower urinary tract symptoms and pelvic pain. He had been diagnosed with an Escherichia coli UTI one month earlier. He had a prior history of treated pulmonary TB. Examination revealed normal prostate and mild suprapubic tenderness. Investigations: Urine microscopy: >100 white cells/μL
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic bacterial prostatitis Pelvic pain and relapsing UTI suggest a deep-seated infection. Prostate exam is normal in chronic bacterial prostatitis and urine tends to be inflammatory with bacteriuria. Prior treatment for TB is a distractor – granulomatous prostatitis is a histologic diagnosis after work-up for an abnormal prostate exam. Chronic pelvic pain syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the recent diagnosis of a UTI with relapse is more suggestive of chronic bacterial prostatitis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q9

questions.question: A man presents with recurrent urinary tract infections and suspected chronic bacterial prostatitis.

parts.text: What is the method to diagnose?
What are the properties of antibiotics that penetrate the prostate?

parts_raw.text: What is the method to diagnosis?
What are the properties of Abx that penetrate the prostate?

questions.model_answer:
a) Lower urinary tract localization studies (Meares-Stamey sequential cultures): VB1 (initial 5-10 mL), VB2 (midstream), EPS expressed by digital prostatic massage, and VB3 (first 5-10 mL immediately after massage). Diagnosis requires the VB3 colony count to exceed VB1 by at least 10-fold, with the same organism recurring in successive UTIs and a negative midstream culture between episodes; microscopy of EPS shows leukocytes and oval fat bodies. Pre- and post-prostate-massage urine cultures are an accepted simplified alternative. Symptoms alone, EPS leukocyte counts alone, or prostate biopsy are inadequate for diagnosis.
b) Agents that cross the prostatic epithelium are those that are lipid-soluble and non-ionized at physiologic pH, minimally protein-bound (only free drug diffuses), small, with a favourable concentration gradient and a pKa allowing ion trapping in prostatic fluid. Fluoroquinolones and TMP-SMX are cited as having superior prostatic penetration, and fosfomycin achieves therapeutic prostatic tissue levels; poor parenchymal penetration is a recognized cause of treatment failure. Note that in ACUTE bacterial prostatitis inflammation permits many drugs that normally do not penetrate to be effective.
c) Guided by susceptibilities: an oral fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin) for at least 4-6 weeks, achieving microbiologic cure in >=70%; TMP-SMX is the alternative preferred oral agent. Oral fosfomycin for MDR E. coli. Long-term suppressive therapy for patients not cured. (In acute prostatitis: FQ or TMP-SMX orally for 2-4 weeks; systemically ill patients get parenteral third-generation cephalosporin or carbapenem +/- aminoglycoside, noting high FQ resistance post-biopsy.)
questions.beyond_mandell: The detailed physicochemical determinants of prostatic penetration (non-ionized lipid-soluble free drug, ion trapping by pKa, low protein binding) are pharmacology-text/urology-literature knowledge; Mandell states only that fluoroquinolones and TMP-SMX have superior prostatic penetration and that fosfomycin achieves therapeutic prostatic levels.

cohort_answer.text: Method: DRE, Prostatic massage with seminal secretions. Properties: Most antibiotics are weak acids/bases that ionize in biological fluids, inhibiting crossing of prostatic epithelium; only free, non-protein-bound molecules enter tissues; prostate capillaries are nonporous; passage enhanced by high concentration gradient, high lipid solubility, low ionization, high pKa, low protein binding, small molecular size. Recommended abx: Fluoroquinolones; Septra; Fosfomycin; Doxycycline.

questions.question: A man presents with recurrent urinary tract infections and suspected chronic bacterial prostatitis.
questions.question_raw: A man with recurrent UTIs – prostatitis

parts.text: Properties of antibiotics to penetrate the prostate
Which antibiotics penetrate the prostate well?

parts_raw.text: Properties of abx to penetrate the prostate
Which antibiotics penetrate the prostate well?

questions.model_answer:
a) Sequential lower urinary tract localization cultures (Meares-Stamey 4-glass test): VB1, VB2, EPS obtained by digital prostatic massage, and VB3 (post-massage voided urine). Bacterial prostatitis is confirmed when the VB3 count exceeds VB1 by >=10-fold with the same organism causing recurrent bacteriuria; EPS microscopy shows leukocytes and oval fat bodies. Pre-/post-massage urine culture is an accepted alternative. In chronic bacterial prostatitis the prostate is usually normal on rectal examination and patients are asymptomatic between episodes; in acute prostatitis the gland is exquisitely tender and vigorous massage is avoided because it may provoke bacteremia.
b) Penetration requires non-protein-bound, lipid-soluble, non-ionized drug crossing the prostatic epithelium, favoured by a high concentration gradient, small molecular size and a pKa permitting ion trapping in prostatic fluid; acute inflammation transiently allows many otherwise non-penetrating drugs to work, while poor parenchymal penetration (along with biofilm, prostatic calculi and altered prostatic fluid pH) underlies failure in chronic disease.
c) Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are the preferred oral agents because of superior prostatic penetration; oral fosfomycin achieves therapeutic prostatic tissue levels and has eradicated MDR Escherichia coli. Doxycycline/azithromycin are used when Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae is implicated in younger sexually active men.
questions.beyond_mandell: The physicochemical penetration criteria and the tetracycline/macrolide prostatic penetration data come from pharmacology and urology literature rather than this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: UCx (post-prostate massage for improved yield), Meares-Stamey 4 glass test; clinical features LUTS, fevers/chills, pelvic/penile tip pain; edematous tender prostate on DRE. Properties: most penetrate during acute inflammatory infection (chronic more challenging); blood-prostate barrier only permits non-protein bound lipophilic abx; low pH allows alkaline abx to concentrate via ionic trapping. Good penetrators: Septra or Cipro/levofloxacin (consider GC/CT coverage if <35y or high risk sexual behaviour); Doxy, Azithro, Fosfomycin also penetrate well

questions.question: You are consulted on a 15-year-old boy who returned from a trip to Eastern Europe 3 weeks ago. During that trip he had a 3-day history of mild viral symptoms (fever, myalgias) that resolved. He also had unprotected sexual intercourse with a partner 6 months ago. He now has testicular pain and you note evidence of orchitis and epididymitis on exam. He also has submandibular tenderness without a mass on exam.
questions.question_raw: You are consulted on a 15yo teenage boy who returned from a trip to Eastern Europe 3 weeks ago. During that trip he had a 3-day history of mild viral symptoms (fever, myalgias) that resolved. He also had unprotected sexual intercourse with a partner 6 months ago. He now has testicular pain and you note evidence of orchitis and epididymitis on exam. He also has submandibular tenderness without a mass on exam.

parts.text: Name 2 microbiologic tests that would confirm the diagnosis

parts_raw.text: Name 2 microbiologic tests that would confirm the diagnosis

questions.model_answer: The picture is mumps orchitis/epididymo-orchitis (viruses, especially mumps, cause most orchitis; orchitis occurs in ~20% of postpubertal males with mumps and may occur without parotid involvement). (1) Mumps virus RT-PCR (and viral culture) on a buccal/parotid duct swab, with urine or CSF as adjunct specimens. (2) Mumps serology - IgM and acute/convalescent IgG seroconversion. Also send urine NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis to exclude sexually transmitted epididymitis.
questions.beyond_mandell: The specific confirmatory assays (buccal swab RT-PCR, IgM/paired IgG serology) follow CDC/PHAC mumps case-definition guidance; this chapter names mumps as the cause but not the tests.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer offers only gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT; the diagnosis to confirm is mumps, so mumps RT-PCR and serology are the tests that establish it.

cohort_answer.text: Likely diagnosis mumps; confirmatory tests: N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis urine NAAT (to rule out other causes of orchitis/epididymitis)
